item.title: The salt in your salary
item.description:
There is a story historians love to tell at dinner parties, the kind that sounds too neat not to be true.
It goes like this: two thousand years ago, a Roman legionary trudged along a dusty road out of the capital, and at the end of his march, his commander didn't hand him coins.
He handed him salt.
A fistful of white crystal, precious enough to trade for bread, wine, even land.
The road they walked came to be called the Via Salaria: the Salt Road.
And the word for what he was owed, salarium, is the direct ancestor of the English word "salary."
It is a wonderful story.
It has been told in classrooms, quoted in dictionaries, repeated in a thousand listicles about the surprising origins of everyday words.
And it is, as far as anyone can tell, mostly untrue.
Start with the crystal, not the coin.
Before Rome existed, speakers of a language nobody ever wrote down -- what linguists now call Proto-Indo-European, spoken somewhere on the Eurasian steppe more than five thousand years ago -- had a word for salt: sal.
Trace its descendants across the map and they barely bother to disguise themselves. Latin kept sal.
Old Irish has salann. Welsh: halen. Old Church Slavonic: solĭ. German still says Salz.
Even Old English's sealt sits just one letter away from the modern word.
Compare that to almost any other piece of five-thousand-year-old vocabulary and the survival rate looks almost miraculous.
Salt, it turns out, was simply too important for anyone to invent a new name for it.
Greek is the one language that plays a trick on you.
It swapped the opening s for an h—hals—the same sound shift that turned an ancient word for "seven" into the Greek hepta.
It isn't a different root pretending to be related. It's the same root, filtered through a sound change that happened in Greek and nowhere else.
Now for Rome, the part everyone gets wrong.
By Augustus's time, salarium had settled into imperial paperwork as the word for a fixed stipend -- the kind paid to provincial governors and the officials around them.
One surviving record shows a proconsul drawing a million sesterces a year under that title.
So far, so administrative.
No salt in sight.
The trouble starts when people go looking for why a word for salt became a word for money, and reach for Pliny the Elder to explain it.
Pliny did write about salt -- pages of it, in Book 31 of his Natural History -- describing how essential it was to daily life and how it even gave Latin its word for wit.
What he never wrote, despite being quoted as saying it in book after book, is that soldiers' pay "was originally salt."
That sentence, in that confident English phrasing, appears nowhere in his surviving text.
It was written in the nineteenth century, attached to Pliny's name, and repeated often enough to survive into respected reference works, including the Lewis and Short Latin Dictionary that generations of Latin students relied upon.
What actually survives from antiquity is much thinner.
Livy mentions a tax the censors imposed in 204 BCE, tied to "the annual salt revenue."
That's a genuine fiscal detail placing salt and money in the same sentence—nothing about soldiers, nothing about rations.
Somewhere in the nineteenth century, that passing reference to a salt tax and Pliny's broader observations became stitched together into one confident story.
The story then outran the evidence by a couple of centuries, and never looked back.
The Oxford Latin Dictionary, to its credit, simply shrugs.
It records salarium, notes its connection to sal, and declines to invent an explanation nobody can prove.
Meanwhile, the word kept moving anyway.
Salarium became Old French salaire, then Anglo-Norman salarie, before appearing in English in the late fourteenth century.
Its earliest confirmed appearance is in Langland's Piers Plowman in 1377 -- not a soldier or a grain of salt anywhere nearby, just a servant complaining that his wages are overdue.
Six hundred and fifty years ago, in its very first documented English sentence, the word already meant almost exactly what your payslip means today.
One trap is worth pointing out before you repeat any of this.
"Salute," "salutation" and "salutary" look like relatives of salt. They're not.
They descend from the Latin salus, meaning health, which comes from a completely different ancestral root meaning "whole."
It's the same root that eventually gave English words like "solid" and, rather grimly, "holocaust."
Salt and salute merely happen to rhyme in English. That's the entire relationship.
Where the salt family holds up without any footnotes is the kitchen.
"Salad" comes from the Roman herba salata, literally, "salted herbs." "Sauce" and "sausage" both descend from salsus, meaning salted.
No fabricated quotations required.
Salt really did that work, plainly, for thousands of years before anyone invented refrigeration.
So the word survived, through five thousand years, a dozen languages and an empire's bureaucracy, while carrying almost none of its original meaning by the time it reached your bank statement.
The story that explains it best isn't the one about the Roman soldier and his fistful of salt.
It's the other one: a made-up quotation, printed with enough confidence in enough dictionaries to outlive the truth by more than 150 years, and counting.

item.title: PM for sustainable housing sector, balanced urban development
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday said the government is committed to building a transparent, accountable and investment-friendly environment for sustainable, planned and corruption-free development of the housing sector.
During a meeting with a delegation of the Real Estate and Housing Association of Bangladesh (REHAB) at the Secretariat, he also said planned and sustainable urbanization is essential for Bangladesh's long-term economic growth, said a release issued by the prime minister’s Press Wing.
The prime minister stressed that urban development should not remain Dhaka-centric, urging greater emphasis on balanced development across the country while protecting agricultural land.
At the meeting, the REHAB delegation discussed the current state of the housing industry, challenges to planned urbanization, practical difficulties arising from the implementation of the Detailed Area Plan (DAP), and measures needed for the sector's long-term development.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman meets a delegation of the Real Estate and Housing Association of Bangladesh (REHAB) at the Secretariat on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. Photo: PM’s Press Wing
The association proposed reducing land, plot and apartment registration fees to a reasonable level to encourage investment in the housing sector.
The delegation also called for the complete digitalisation of government services related to the real estate sector to improve efficiency and transparency.
The REHAB leaders urged the government to rationally increase the Floor Area Ratio (FAR) and promote vertical urban development to ensure the best use of limited land, particularly in the capital.
Addressing the delegation, Tarique Rahman described the housing sector as one of the key drivers of the national economy.
"The development of the housing sector is vital for the country's overall economic growth. The government is working to establish a transparent, accountable and investment-friendly environment where the housing industry can grow in a planned, sustainable and corruption-free manner," he said.
The prime minister said the government has already undertaken a series of reform initiatives to prevent irregularities in the housing sector and that further effective measures are being prepared.
He also emphasized the need to expand planned urbanisation beyond Dhaka.
"Urban development should not remain centred only on Dhaka. Other regions of the country must also be developed in a planned manner with equal importance," Tarique Rahman said, adding that agricultural land must be protected alongside development activities.
Housing and Public Works Minister Zakaria Taher attended the meeting along with REHAB President Dr Ali Afzal, Vice-President-2 Abu Khalid Md Barkatullah and senior representatives of leading real estate companies, including Eastern Housing Ltd, United Group, Rupayan Group, Amin Mohammad Group, Century Group, US-Bangla Assets Ltd and Swadesh Properties Ltd.

More than a decade after the human microbiome was comprehensively mapped, scientists have now identified the vast communities of microbes that make up the Great Barrier Reef.

item.description:
Figures come as large parts of southern Europe endure another record-breaking period of extreme temperatures

France recorded more than 5,700 excess deaths during its June heatwave, authorities have said, as swathes of southern Europe continue to endure another record-breaking period of extreme temperatures.

The French national health agency said on Wednesday that it had recorded 5,764 excess deaths ⁠between ​17 June and 2 July, an excess mortality rate of 36%.

item.title: Trump administration says 15 agencies will get $5bn in ‘AI for science’ effort
item.description:
Administration will also overhaul how US government funds federal research by supporting individual scientists and AI over universities

The US will spend $5bn to tackle longstanding scientific problems across multiple fields using AI, ⁠the Trump administration said in a statement on Wednesday. The agencies will use the funding to identify the root causes ⁠of chronic diseases, accelerate drug ⁠discovery and ​develop longer-lasting building materials, among other tasks, according to the statement.

Scientists will have access to the Department of Energy’s supercomputers, AI and specialized ⁠datasets, along with other components needed to run experiments using algorithms, said Michael Kratsios, chief technology adviser to Donald Trump, in an ⁠interview with Reuters.

item.title: Two decades of mass protests in India
item.description:
Thousands of supporters of India’s youth-led “cockroach” movement have been protesting since June, demanding the education minister resign over exam paper leaks, in the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his third term.

Activists say the leaks showed widespread corruption, a complaint which has brought crowds onto the streets for years. Following are details of major rallies, triggered by graft and other crimes and causes, over the past two decades.

April 2011

Anti-corruption activist Anna Hazare started the first of two hunger strikes in a bid to push the government to bring in anti-graft legislation.

Hundreds of thousands rallied to his support across the country and he was briefly jailed by the then-Congress alliance government.

India’s parliament eventually passed an anti-graft law, though Hazare said it watered down his demands. Some of his supporters went on to form the Aam Aadmi Party in 2012, now one of Modi’s opponents in parliament.

December 2012

Public fury over the gang-rape of a young woman on a moving bus in New Delhi erupted into mass protests in the capital.

Crowds blockaded roads, broke through police lines in street confrontations and called for an overhaul of a system and a society they said had failed to tackle violence against women. Many demanded the culprits be executed.

The 23-year-old woman died in a Singapore hospital a few days after the attack. In response, India amended laws to expand the definition of sexual assault and set up fast-track courts to speed up trials in such cases.

December 2019

India’s parliament passed a new citizenship law that brought hundreds of thousands of people to the streets in protests and triggered bouts of sectarian violence that killed at least 76 people.

The Citizenship Amendment Act aimed to fast-track citizenship for Hindus, Parsis, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains and Christians who arrived in India on or before December 31, 2014 from neighbouring Muslim-majority Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

Critics said the law, alongside a proposed national register of citizens, discriminated against Muslims and violated the spirit of India’s secular constitution. Some feared the government would remove the citizenship of Muslims without documents in some border states.

India implemented the law in March 2024.

September 2020

Thousands of farmers blocked roads and railway tracks in protests against new legislation that they say could pave the way for the government to stop buying grain at guaranteed prices, leaving them at the mercy of private buyers.

Modi’s government defended the bills, saying they would help rid India’s vast agriculture sector of antiquated laws and allow farmers to sell to institutional buyers and big retailers.

The protests lasted more than a year before Modi repealed the laws.

June 2022

An overhaul of military recruitment, designed to bring in fitter, younger troops and reduce pension expenditure, triggered rail blockades and protests across the country.

Recruits, veterans and opposition leaders objected to the introduction of fixed four-year contracts, saying people would struggle to get other jobs once their service was over.

Modi’s government refused to roll back the programme but offered instead to reserve 10 per cent of state vacancies for those who had served the four years.

August 2024

Thousands of doctors took to the streets for months after the rape and murder of a trainee doctor in a government hospital in the eastern city of Kolkata.

Protesters demanded safer workplaces, a crackdown on violence against women and a swift investigation into the attack.

item.title: The Karim Khan saga: a timeline
item.description:
The Karim Khan saga: a timeline

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Thu, 07/23/2026 - 14:09
How allegations against the ICC’s chief prosecutor became entangled with pressure over his pursuit of Israeli officials, culminating in a vote that could reshape the court
Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on 14 March 2025 (AFP/file photo)
Off

Member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) are due to vote at the United Nations' headquarters in New York on Friday on whether to remove the court's chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, from office – a first in the court’s 24-year history. 

The vote caps a saga stretching back more than two years, spanning sexual misconduct allegations Khan has consistently denied, a UN-led investigation, a judicial panel that unanimously cleared him, and a bureau that chose to override that finding and press ahead regardless.

The case has unfolded alongside a separate campaign of pressure on Khan and the court over his pursuit of war crimes warrants against Israeli and Hamas leaders, from a threat by Britain's then foreign secretary to defund the ICC, to sanctions imposed on Khan and dozens of ICC officials by the Trump administration, to the US secretary of state's public vow to "dismantle" the court.

Khan, a British barrister, is the ICC's third chief prosecutor since the court’s founding in 2002. 

In addition to seeking warrants for Israeli leaders, his office has sought arrest warrants for Russia’s Vladimir Putin, the Philippines' Rodrigo Duterte, Myanmar’s junta leaders, and Taliban officials in Afghanistan. 

Middle East Eye has been at the forefront of exclusive coverage of the misconduct case at all stages.

Below is a timeline of how the case unfolded, from early 2024 till the highly controversial 24 July vote.

Palestine investigation, and the pressure campaign begins (2021–2023)

February 2021 Karim Khan is elected ICC chief prosecutor by the Assembly of States Parties (ASP). 

March 2021 Khan's predecessor, Fatou Bensouda, opens the ICC's investigation into alleged war crimes in the occupied Palestinian territories.

21 June 2021 Khan takes the oath of office, becoming the third person to hold the post since the court's founding in 2002.

Summer 2022 The woman who later becomes the complainant in the sexual misconduct case alleges a separate senior ICC official behaved inappropriately towards her.

31 August 2022 Khan writes to the ASP president raising her concerns about that other official; external investigators are appointed in October 2022 with her cooperation.

11 December 2023 That separate external investigation concludes there was "no unsatisfactory conduct" by the official concerned.

17 November 2023 Five states (South Africa, Bangladesh, Bolivia, Comoros, Djibouti) formally refer the Palestine situation to the prosecutor after the 7 October Hamas attack on Israel and the subsequent Israeli war on Gaza.

December 2023 Khan visits Israel (kibbutzim, the Nova festival site) and meets Palestinian officials including President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah. 

Lead-up to the warrants (January–April 2024)

January 2024 Khan convenes an independent, seven-member expert panel to assess whether the legal threshold for arrest warrants for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his then Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, and three Hamas leaders had been met. The panel unanimously concludes in March the process was "fair, rigorous and independent" and sufficient material existed to request warrants.

16 March 2024 Khan's legal team concludes it will be in a position to apply for the Israeli and Hamas warrants by the end of April.

21 March 2024 Khan orders a "complementarity" check into whether Israel was investigating the alleged crimes itself; his office concludes it was not.

ICC issues arrest warrants for Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant
Read More »

25 March 2024 Khan informs the US administration of his decision and that warrants would be sought by the end of April.

15 April 2024 In London, Khan tells UK Justice Secretary Alex Chalk he will apply for the warrants; he had wanted to brief Foreign Secretary David Cameron directly, but Cameron was abroad.

19 April 2024 A senior US official warns Khan by phone of "disastrous consequences" if he proceeds; Khan says he rejected this, citing Israel's lack of cooperation.

23 April 2024 While Khan is on an official visit to Venezuela, Cameron phones him and says issuing warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant would be "like dropping a hydrogen bomb". Cameron spoke aggressively, told Khan he would "lose the dressing room" and be seen as "losing the plot", and said the UK would "defund the court and withdraw from the Rome Statute" if warrants were issued. Khan replied that this would mean "the rules-based system would be dead".

In an account of the episode in MEE journalist Peter Oborne's book, Complicit: Britain’s Role in the Destruction of Gaza, a source close to Cameron said that the call with Khan did take place and was “robust”. But the source said that rather than making a threat, Cameron pointed out that strong voices in the Conservative Party would push for defunding the ICC and withdrawing from the Rome Statute.

24 April 2024 12 Republican US senators (including Marco Rubio) send Khan a letter warning "Target Israel and we will target you." 

25 April 2024 British journalist Douglas Murray writes in the New York Post that Khan will seek warrants within days, before this is public knowledge.

26 April 2024 Netanyahu publicly criticises the ICC on social media, saying: “Under my leadership, Israel will never accept any attempt by the ICC to undermine its inherent right of self-defence.”

28 April 2024 Israel says it will allow Khan to visit Israel and Gaza, an unprecedented offer that delays the warrant applications.

29 April 2024 A colleague of Khan's raises harassment allegations against him in a private conversation.

30 April–1 May 2024 Khan describes meetings with western states and US officials that he characterises as efforts to dissuade him from proceeding.

Warrants filed, allegations surface (May 2024)

2 May 2024 The sexual misconduct/harassment allegations are first put to Khan in person by members of his team, on the same day, per his later ICC submission, that he had been planning to announce the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants. Khan separately meets Dutch counterterrorism officials over a security briefing about suspected Mossad activity in The Hague.

Exclusive: How Karim Khan’s Israel war crimes probe was derailed by threats, leaks and sex claims
Read More »

3 May 2024 A colleague of Khan refers the harassment allegations to the ICC's Internal Oversight Mechanism (IOM).

7 May 2024 The IOM's first inquiry closes after the complainant declines to cooperate.

19–20 May 2024 With Israel's promised permission letter for the Gaza visit still not delivered, Khan cancels the trip and, on 20 May, announces he is seeking arrest warrants for Netanyahu, Gallant, and Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar, Ismail Haniyeh and Mohammed Deif. In his public statement he says: "I insist that all attempts to impede, intimidate or improperly influence the officials of this Court must cease immediately."

21 May 2024 David Cameron publicly calls the warrant decision "a mistake", accusing the ICC of drawing a "moral equivalence" between Israeli and Hamas leaders.

10 June 2024 The outgoing Conservative government files a formal objection disputing ICC jurisdiction over Israeli nationals; the incoming Labour government drops the objection the following month, after the July 2024 general election.

Leaks, a second complaint, arrest warrants (October–November 2024)

17 October 2024 An anonymous Twitter account begins circulating details of the harassment allegations against Khan.

19 October 2024 The Mail on Sunday reports that ASP President Paivi Kaukoranta has confirmed the allegations exist; an official ASP statement follows later on 24 October.

October–November 2024 A second IOM investigation opens and closes after the complainant again declines to cooperate. 

11 November 2024 The ASP president subsequently decides to seek an outsourced UN investigation into Khan via the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS).

21 November 2024 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously approves and issues the arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant, the first time the court has targeted officials of a western-allied state. It also rejected two Israeli challenges to the case under Articles 19 and 18 of the Rome Statute.

Sanctions and threats (February–August 2025)

6 February 2025 Trump issues Executive Order 14203 imposing sanctions on ICC officials, with Khan as the initial target, over the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants; his US visa is revoked, his wife and children are barred from the US, and UK bank accounts are frozen.

19 May 2025 Khan takes voluntary leave pending the OIOS investigation; deputy prosecutors Nazhat Shameem Khan and Mame Mandiaye Niang take over the leadership of his office. 

May 2025 Shortly before going on leave, Khan had been preparing new warrant applications for Israeli ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir over West Bank settlement expansion.

‘Financial death penalty’: How US sanctions are upending the lives of ICC judges
Read More »

5 June 2025 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announces sanctions against four ICC judges: Beti Hohler (Slovenia) and Reine Alapini-Gansou (Benin) for their role in the Netanyahu/Gallant arrest warrants; and Luz del Carmen Ibanez Carranza (Peru) and Solomy Balungi Bossa (Uganda) for authorising the Afghanistan investigation. 

9 July 2026 The US sanctions UN Special Rapporteur on Palestine Francesca Albanese over her cooperation with the ICC. 

16 July 2025 ICC judges reject an Israeli request to withdraw the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants pending Israel's jurisdictional appeal.

20 August 2025 US imposes sanctions on judges Kimberly Prost (Canada) and Nicolas Yann Guillou (France), plus deputy prosecutors Nazhat Shameem Khan (Fiji) and Mame Mandiaye Niang (Senegal).

4 September 2025 US sanctions three Palestinian NGOs for cooperating with the ICC. 

13 October 2025 MEE reveals that Margareta Kassangana, a Polish diplomat and ASP vice president, met privately with Khan's accuser to discuss the case before the Bureau of the Assembly of States Parties, the court's govening body, referred the matter to the UN's OIOS in late 2024.

MEE also reports on a recorded summer 2025 phone call in which another bureau member, Uganda's ambassador Mirjam Blaak, is heard telling a colleague she believed Khan "may not come back", describing the complainant in personal terms, and repeating Netanyahu's since-debunked claim that Khan rushed the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants to pre-empt a "honey trap" defence. 

Disqualification bid and secret Smotrich filing (November 2025–May 2026)

17 November 2025 Israel formally asks the ICC to disqualify Khan from the Palestine investigation and withdraw the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants, citing the misconduct allegations as evidence of bias. The court has yet to rule on the request.

3 December 2025 The ASP's annual assembly in The Hague issues a declaration resisting US demands to drop the Palestine/Afghanistan investigations and amend the Rome Statute, without naming the US directly.

Exclusive: ICC prosecutor's office seeks arrest warrant for Israel's Smotrich
Read More »

10 December 2025 Khan submits a statement to the ICC's appeal chamber responding to Israel's disqualification request, describing for the first time a "senior UK government official" (confirmed by MEE as Cameron) who threatened UK funding withdrawal.

11 December 2025 The OIOS delivers its finalised report (150 pages, with roughly 5,000 pages of supporting evidence) to the ASP-appointed judicial panel for a legal determination.

18 December 2025 The US sanctions judges Gocha Lordkipanidze (Georgia) and Erdenebalsuren Damdin (Mongolia) after their rejection of Israel's appeal against the Gaza investigation.

22 January 2026 Responding to a Freedom of Information request, the UK Foreign Office confirms for the first time that the Cameron–Khan call took place on 23 April 2024.

9 March 2026 MEE breaks the story that a three-judge panel (Leona Theron of South Africa, Paul Lemmens of Belgium and Seymour Panton of Jamaica) unanimously concludes the OIOS findings "do not establish misconduct or breach of duty" by Khan. Lemmens, in a separate opinion, says he has "serious doubts" the allegations could ever meet the required standard, but joins the unanimous conclusion. 

23 March 2026 MEE reports that some bureau member states seek to sabotage the judges' panel's report. 

2 April 2026 A majority of the bureau votes to disregard the panel's conclusion and make its own assessment of the evidence. MEE names the 15 states that voted this way as Belgium, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Cyprus, Ecuador, Finland, Italy, Japan, Latvia, New Zealand, Poland, Slovenia, South Korea and Switzerland.

2 April 2026 The prosecutor's office secretly files an arrest warrant application for Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, alleging war crimes, crimes against humanity, and apartheid over West Bank settlement policy. It was the same warrant prepared by Khan before he went on leave but, as MEE reported, it was shelved for about a year.

Khan speaks out publicly for first time (April–May 2026)

29 April 2026 Khan gives his first public comments since going on leave, in an interview with journalist Mehdi Hasan on the outlet Zeteo. He says he thought the judges' panel finding "was the end of the matter" and is "perplexed" the bureau didn't close the case immediately. He calls the theory that he rushed the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants to distract from the allegations "baloney", noting that he told the US and others he would seek warrants in March 2024, before any allegation was raised. He says Russian and Israeli intelligence had been conducting "close surveillance" of him. 

8 May 2026 In an interview with MEE’s David Hearst Podcast, Khan accuses bureau members of running a "dangerous", biased campaign against him and says the disciplinary process is a "Khan-made process... specific to me".

Bureau's decision, run-up to vote (June–July 2026)

8 June 2026 The bureau votes to suspend Khan and, by a two-thirds majority, finds he committed "serious misconduct". MEE reports the vote as 14 in favour (Belgium, Brazil, Chile, Cyprus, Ecuador, Finland, Italy, Japan, Latvia, New Zealand, Poland, Slovenia, South Korea, Switzerland), four against (Kenya, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Uganda), three abstaining (Bolivia, Bosnia, South Africa).

The confidential decision, seen by MEE, frames the finding as Khan having "engaged in a sexual relationship" with the complainant that was improper given the power imbalance, a notable shift from the original non-consensual-conduct allegation. Khan denies any sexual relationship; the complainant's account centres on non-consensual conduct. Khan's lawyers say this reframed allegation was never put to him.

18 June 2026 MEE reveals the bureau has set 24 July, at UN headquarters in New York, as the date and venue for the full ASP's special session.

13 July 2026 US Secretary of State Marco Rubio explicitly threatens that Washington would "dismantle the ICC – brick by brick, if necessary".

16 July 2026 CNN airs an interview with Khan’s accuser going public for the first time, standing by her allegations of non-consensual sex. 

17 July 2026 ASP President Kaukoranta writes to member states confirming the bureau failed to reach the required majority on two separate retaliation allegations against Khan (from other staff members), which are now closed as unproven, distinct from the sexual misconduct finding still going to the full Assembly.

18 July 2026 Josep Borrell, the former EU foreign policy chief, writes that the bureau's process amounts to a "political vote" serving what he calls a US-Israeli "offensive" to "defang" the court, citing Rubio's stated intent to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick".

21 July 2026 Khan's legal team issues an open letter to ASP members stating that formal channels for Khan to make representations have been closed, that the ASP president discouraged states from meeting with his team, and that Khan and his lawyers have been denied accreditation to attend the 24 July session.

24 July 2026 (scheduled) The full ASP votes by secret ballot at UN headquarters, New York, under Article 46 of the Rome Statute, on the single combined motion covering both the misconduct finding and Khan's removal.

item.title: Govt working to normalise gas supply after FSRU technical fault
item.description:
The government is working to restore normal gas supply across the country after a technical fault at a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) disrupted the national gas distribution system.

The malfunction has reduced gas supply to the national grid by around 450 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd), the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources said in a statement today, Thursday.

Gas supply from the affected FSRU has been temporarily suspended due to the technical glitch, resulting in low gas pressure for industrial units, power plants, CNG filling stations and other consumers in different parts of the country.

The ministry said relevant agencies and technical experts are working round the clock to resolve the problem as quickly as possible.

Meanwhile, efforts are being made to ensure uninterrupted gas supply to emergency and priority sectors through optimal management of the available supply.

The statement noted that inadequate emphasis on domestic gas exploration and production in previous years increased the country's dependence on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG), making the national gas supply system vulnerable to disruptions whenever import infrastructure encounters operational problems.

To reduce that dependence, the government has undertaken short-, medium- and long-term initiatives to boost domestic gas production. As part of the plan, 100 gas wells will be drilled in phases across the country.

It also mentioned that the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) today, Thursday approved a Tk 7.29 billion project for drilling three gas wells in Begumganj and Sunamganj.

According to the statement, efforts are also underway to accelerate gas exploration in both onshore and offshore areas by inviting bids under the Production Sharing Contract (PSC) framework and encouraging investment from local and foreign companies.

The ministry added that gas exploration, well drilling, infrastructure development and the start of commercial production require considerable time, adding that the government is treating the issue as a top priority.

As part of its broader energy security strategy, the government has also initiated measures including inviting tenders for a fourth FSRU, assessing the feasibility of importing LNG from Malaysia through ISO tanks, reviewing pipeline and other transportation options to bring Bhola gas to the mainland, drilling new wells and carrying out workovers at existing gas fields, and diversifying energy import sources and supply infrastructure.

item.title: Experts for inclusive instant payment system to boost remittances, financial inclusion
item.description:
Financial sector leaders, central bank officials, and researchers gathered in Dhaka today to discuss how an Inclusive Instant Payment System (IIPS) could transform Bangladesh’s financial ecosystem by lowering transaction costs, reducing reliance on informal remittance channels, and driving digital inclusion.
The inception workshop, titled “Analysis of the Inclusive Instant Payment System (IIPS) in Bangladesh and Cross-Border Remittance as a Use Case,” was organized by the Policy Research Institute of Bangladesh (PRI) with support from the Gates Foundation.
Opening the session, PRI chairman Zaidi Sattar emphasized the critical macroeconomic role of remittances, which currently account for roughly 6% of Bangladesh’s GDP.
He called for strategic policies to shift these financial flows from basic consumption toward productive investment.
Sattar also highlighted the ongoing digital divide, pointing out that many migrant workers—such as the roughly 700,000 Bangladeshis living in Oman—still prefer informal hundi channels over formal banking due to existing barriers.
Addressing the technical groundwork, Mohammad Jahid Iqbal, additional director of the Payment System Department at Bangladesh Bank, revealed that the central bank is developing the IIPS using the open-source Mojaloop platform.
Launched in November 2025, the system aims to lower costs and connect banks, payment service providers, and eventually microfinance institutions.
It will also feature-phone access, simplified account opening, reduced transaction failures, and enhanced fraud protection using the Tazama toolkit.
Presenting research on the topic, PRI research director Bazlul Haque Khondker explained that an IIPS would make the payment ecosystem truly interoperable across banks and mobile financial services (MFS). Real-time, low-cost payment corridors could significantly curb reliance on informal channels and generate major savings for households.
PRI director MA Razzaque added that formalizing remittances will strengthen household resilience and national foreign-exchange reserves. To better understand migrant behaviors regarding speed, exchange rates, and trust, PRI is conducting a survey of Bangladeshi migrants across six key destination countries to inform practical policy solutions.
Single strategy for a cashless future
Ezazul Islam, director general of BIBM, noted that the long-term success of the IIPS will require a robust governance framework, fair commercial incentives, effective dispute resolution, and sound settlement risk management.
Sayed Shaikh Ibna Jilany, vice president of remittance at bKash Limited, added that private-sector integration must prioritize consumer protection, affordability, and user trust.
Ahsan H Mansur, distinguished fellow at PRI, argued that financial inclusion, IIPS deployment, and the transition toward a cashless economy must be treated as a single, unified national strategy.
He revealed that Bangladesh Bank currently spends approximately Tk20,000 crore annually on cash management—a cost that continues to rise.
To accelerate the shift to digital, he suggested that temporary incentives or subsidies for digital payments could offer greater long-term economic returns than subsidies in other sectors.
He also called for measures to make smartphones and internet services more affordable, restore public confidence in the banking sector, and create dedicated investment mechanisms to help repatriate an estimated $2 billion to $3 billion from the Bangladeshi diaspora.

One week after the United States and Israel killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and ignited a regional war, drones started flying over Basra in southern Iraq. They were targeting Iraq’s oil industry. They hit an oilfield operated by BP, as well as a cargo terminal at Basra airport and a large compound that houses foreign companies that service the oil sector. Another attack on 6 March hit the same compound, striking offices and warehouses used by Halliburton and KBR, two US companies that have been in Iraq since the 2003 invasion. The attack sparked a massive fire that lit up the night sky.

In the wider war, it was not a particularly notable day – but in Iraq the strikes laid bare just how weak the state had become and “how easily sovereignty could be violated”, as one senior Iraqi security official put it to me. For 40 years, the US, Iran and Israel existed in an uneasy equilibrium of neither peace nor war. As this has come to a sudden, dramatic end, Iraq finds itself caught in the middle.

item.title: The Guardian view on Britain’s uninhabitable homes: as temperatures rise, a new approach is needed | Editorial
item.description:
Sadiq Khan’s heat-ready plan for London is a sensible strategy for adaptation that should provide a roadmap for other cities

“Our ability to trust that our homes will keep us safe from the outside is under threat,” the geographer Sam Johnson-Schlee writes in Hot House, his recent book on how heat has transformed domestic life. This summer, high temperatures have become inescapable. People have coped with makeshift solutions: keeping curtains drawn, placing foil over windows or – for those who can afford one – plugging in an air-conditioning unit. Planning experts warn that, with only about half of councils requiring new buildings to include cooling strategies, many homes will become “death traps” as temperatures rise.

Britain’s homes weren’t built to cope with this. The country’s historically mild climate allowed developers to build houses without insulation, while industrialisation supplied plentiful coal to burn when temperatures dropped. Many homes are consequently drafty in winter and sweltering in summer. Unlike those in Mediterranean climates, British homes lack shutters and shaded communal spaces. While Ildefons Cerdà, Barcelona’s masterplanner, was designing housing blocks with cool courtyards and chamfered edges to allow breezes to flow, Britain’s Victorian builders were throwing up rows of terrace houses – many without cross-ventilation – and giving little thought to the movement of the sun.

item.title: The Guardian view on Europe’s demographic crisis: the young must not be left to deal with the consequences | Editorial
item.description:
A new Brussels study highlights the pace at which EU countries are ageing. A more informed public debate is overdue

Europe is ageing at pace as birthrates fall and people live longer. A new report by the European Commission, published this month, notes that 2012 marked the first year in which fewer people were born in EU countries than people died in them. By the middle of this century, nearly one in three EU residents will be 65 or older. The numbers of those over 80 will almost triple from 6% to 15%. The old continent is getting visibly greyer.

The transition to a “longevity society”, as the report’s authors describe it, is something to be celebrated. Many people are enjoying healthier, richer lives for longer, and redefining the meaning and possibilities of old age. But the statistics and direction of travel also point to immense social challenges, with implications for the way we work, intergenerational fairness and the future funding of care. Sadly, amid fraught and at times toxic debates about immigration and the cost of welfare, Europe’s politics is struggling to meet the moment.
